title: Voice (sustained sung vowels)
reference_instrument: adult male voice, sustained vowels (VocalSet long tones, CC BY 4.0)
summary: Sustained vowels on C3, C4 and F4, with no words. On all 14 graded notes the tract is another man's, from MRI of spoken German vowels, so the tilt follows the subject's vowels, not the singers'. Harmonics-to-noise is inside its loose ruler on 14 of 14 pages, but the shape is wrong even where the total is right. A vocal fold model self-oscillates against that tract (two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, with a tapered rest gap on C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid, F4-e and F4-o, and Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold on F4-a), and the sound is read at a simulated microphone 0.30 m from the mouth, 45 degrees off axis, with a rigid sphere for the head and a larger one for the torso under it on the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes; C3-a and F4-a, on the cards restored from 2026-11-05, radiate through a baffled opening. C3-a alone also carries a nasal tract, open at the velum: another speaker's measured nasal passages and maxillary sinuses (Dang, Honda and Suzuki 1994; Dang and Honda 1996), with the port area from one baritone's CT (Sundberg et al. 2004). No source waveform or formant filter is applied. On two of the graded notes (C3-e and C4-o) the breath pressure acts at the far end of a branched airway below the folds, Weibel's symmetric tree with measured dimensions, whose walls carry the vocal-tract wall as a stand-in; on the other twelve it acts straight under the glottis. Twelve pages were restored on 2026-11-10 to earlier renders (F4-e twice); ten still play them, and the first item below says which rows each carries. One scale on the fold stiffnesses (Q on the body-cover fold; on C4-e, Q scales the fold's masses, thicknesses and springs together by Ishizaka and Flanagan's printed tension law) is the one model-only factor: trimmed on the model alone, it puts each card near its written note, so pitch isn't evidence. The graded notes are straight tones with a slow and a fast pitch row, a small cycle-to-cycle shimmer in the glottal pulse, and no vibrato. The phrases carry vibrato, with both pitch rows and the shimmer under it, and each vowel there is its own render, joined by crossfades. The /a/ at six pitches and the vowel ladder further down are older renders on earlier tracts.
physics_present: Restored pages (2026-11-10, deploy 786, and since deploy 793 each playing its clip as first processed, by the owner's ruling that a page changes only at or above the note's best count, and on a tie only if the total distance does not grow): twelve pages were put back to earlier renders, each with its own page text, and ten still play them. The counts are loose, then strict, on the grader of 2026-11-10 with each clip graded once, against the later page each replaced; a total distance is the sum over the measures of each gap over its largest loose ruler value. C3-a (set voice/C3-a-shimmer, rendered 2026-11-05; 13 and 12, against 10 and 10; since moved to a render of 2026-11-10 of the same card with the nasal rows added, set voice/C3-a-nasal, 14 and 14, the nasal item below) and F4-a (set voice/F4-a-bodycover, rendered 2026-11-05, the body-cover fold at Q 4.109; 9 and 9, against 4 and 4) carry the subject's tract, the slow and fast pitch rows, the pulse shimmer, the 192 kHz fold clock, the Verge 1995 flue-jet noise row, humid body-temperature air in the tract, the cited wall (the Flanagan setting as given by Birkholz, Haesner and Kuerbis 2022) and a baffled circular opening at the microphone. They lack the measured wall, the alveolar air, the constriction_noise row, the head, the torso, the head_load row, the observer_law absorption and the branched airway, and C3-a lacks the tapered rest gap. Seven pages play renders of 2026-11-08 (sets voice/<note>-wall): C3-i (10 and 10, against 7 and 7), C3-o (14 and 13, against 12 and 11), C3-u (7 and 7, against 6 and 5), C4-u (14 and 14, against 8 and 8) and C4-u-rigid (14 and 14, against 8 and 8), and, by the tie rule, C4-i (15 and 14, the count of the airway page it replaced, total distance 9.49 against 9.69) and F4-o (15 and 15, the count of its airway page, 5.84 against 6.37). F4-e was put back to its wall render (12 and 9, against 11 and 6) and has since gone back further by the tie rule, to its render of 2026-11-08 before the wall (set voice/F4-e-foldshape; 12 and 9, 11.01 against 11.40). C4-e (9 and 9, against 7 and 7) was put back the same way and has since moved to a render of 2026-11-10 on the same card with the fold on the tension law (the retrim item below), 10 and 10, with the same rows. The wall pages and C4-e carry the measured wall, the alveolar air, the constriction_noise row, the head, the torso, the head_load row and the observer_law absorption, the tapered rest gap on C3-u, C4-u, C4-u-rigid and F4-o, the subject's tense /u/ on C3-u and the lax /u/ on C4-u and C4-u-rigid. They lack the branched airway. C4-a (set voice/C4-a-foldshape, rendered 2026-11-08; 12 and 12, the count of the page it replaced, which played a trained singer's sung /a/ with the measured wall and the branched airway, 10.85 against 12.67) and F4-e carry the same rows as the wall pages except the measured wall: both carry the cited wall, with the tapered rest gap, and C4-a plays the subject's tense /a/. The two pages not restored (C3-e and C4-o) carry the wall pages' rows and the branched airway, with the tapered rest gap on C3-e.

On the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, two-mass vocal folds on Ishizaka and Flanagan's 1972 law as printed, for the glottal flow and the forces on the masses, as a mirror pair, with masses and base stiffnesses from the licensed model-card pack. The oscillation isn't imposed: it comes from the fold, the flow, collision and the tract loop.

Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold (NCVS Status and Progress Report 6, 1994), case C of their Table 1, with that report's own pressure and flow law, on F4-a only. Q, one scale on its four stiffnesses, is the one model-only factor: trimmed to within 3 cents of the written note, it ended at 4.109 against a start of 4.633, and the live F4-a page is that render (restored on 2026-11-10); on later renders that are not live, Q moved x 0.813 for the measured wall, to 3.340, and x 2.267 for the airway, to 7.572. Story and Titze's 0.8 kPa lung pressure isn't applied; the breath stays the card's player row. The fold misses its own paper's Table 2 on this model's test tube, and the paper's tube isn't printed. The other twelve pages it was tried on keep the two-mass fold: on the five C3 pages the measured tract holds its pitch off the note; on C4-a, C4-o, C4-u and F4-o its pitch jumps across the note between nearly equal values of Q; and C4-e, C4-i and F4-e reached their notes but didn't pass the posting rule. Re-tried on F4-e on the cards of 11-07, trimmed again to within 3 cents (Q 6.983), it moved the partial frequencies from 9.2 to 4.4 cents off the recording's and the period swing over the middle of the clip from 37.0 to 20.8 cents (5-95 %) against the recording's 19.8, and it raised the count from 5 to 6 of 14, but its harmonics-to-noise overshot the recording, 28.6 against 25.4 dB, a gap 1.06 dB wider, past the ruler's smallest value of 0.70, so it doesn't post. On the measured C3 tracts this fold's pitch stays at 125–157 Hz whatever its stiffness (Q 0.45–1.29); on a plain 17.5 cm tube the same fold at the same breath sings 108–114 Hz. The tract holds its pitch, so there are no C3 pages.

On C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid, F4-e and F4-o, the two-mass fold takes the self-oscillating form of Birkholz, Kröger and Neuschaefer-Rube (2011): the masses move rigidly and the rest gap narrows to nothing at the front of the folds. The row has no number in it. On each of those pages the three fold stiffnesses were trimmed again for it, to within 3 cents of the written note, and both pitch rows were scaled once by the new gain. F4-o posted it on 2026-11-05 as an exception to that lane's posting rule; C3-a, C3-e, C3-u, C4-a, C4-u, C4-u-rigid and F4-e posted it on 2026-11-08 by the count rule, a tie or a rise; C3-a's page was restored on 2026-11-10 to a render of 2026-11-05 without it, and its nasal render of 2026-11-10 is on that card. On C3-i, C3-o, C4-e, C4-i and C4-o it was tried the same day and the count fell (C3-i 10 to 7, C3-o 14 to 11, C4-e 9 to 8, C4-i 15 to 14, C4-o 12 to 9), so those pages keep the uniform gap. F4-a's body-cover fold doesn't take the row.

A measured tract on every page: subject 1 of the Dresden Vocal Tract Dataset (Birkholz et al. 2020, CC0), a man in MRI of spoken German vowels, tense or lax by a rule fixed before any grade. The subject's tense /u/ on C3-u and in both phrases needs the glottal line's ceiling of 131072 taps, one doubling over the default, at the same tolerances. C4-u and C4-u-rigid play the subject's lax /u/, the pages restored on 2026-11-10; the tense /u/ was tried on both and is listed under what is missing. The cut from the subject's 3-D model to one dimension is this model's own (91 to 115 sections), and the dataset's own printed area functions aren't used.

A nasal tract on C3-a only (the velum, nasal_section, nasal_pair, sinus and nostrils rows, posted on 2026-11-10 at 14 and 14 against the note's best of 13 and 12): the velopharyngeal port is open at 0.15 cm2, joining the tract after its section 40 (0-based). That area is the one measured port area on a sung vowel the hunt found: Sundberg, Birch, Gumoes, Prytz, Karle and Stavad (NCVS notes 2004, p. 3; J Voice 21(2):127-137, 2007), one professional baritone holding the posture for a CT scan of about 40 s 'as for singing the vowel [a]', not confirmed phonating, pitch not stated, and sung on another occasion. The nasal passages (a common passage of 13 sections, then a left and a right passage of 24 sections each, all 3 mm long) and the two maxillary sinuses (16.1 and 16.5 cm3, ostia 0.076 and 0.065 cm2, 43 mm from the nostrils) are another speaker's, borrowed onto this subject's tract: Dang, Honda and Suzuki (1994) Fig. 6, subject Sub.2, digitized from the figure, a declared stand-in, and Dang and Honda (1996), each sinus a lumped cavity. The nostrils take this subject's subnasale from the Dresden MRI, 27.63 mm above the mouth's centre (by a rule chosen after seeing the profile, MB 18119) and 7.07 mm either side, the right naris measured and mirrored; they radiate in the mouth's plane, although the subnasale sits 12.27 mm in front of it. Assumed for the nose: the oral tract's wall, gas and loss, and no loading between the three openings. Each opening's flow reaches the microphone through its own line, sized by its own convergence ladder: 524288 taps at the lips (11 rungs), 1048576 at the left nostril and 524288 at the right. The card was not retrimmed after the nasal rows were added: the page sits 7.9 c above the written note, where the same card without them sat 2.0 c below, and its attack time left its ruler (3.34 against 3.24) while the spectrum and the band envelope came inside theirs. The same nasal rows were tried on F4-a on 2026-11-10 and not posted: added to its live body-cover card with no other row moved and no retrim, on a binary that renders the card without them byte for byte as the page's raw render, they read 7 and 7 against the note's best of 9 and 9 (total distance 12.6845 against 10.6039). The pitch rose 79.5 c over the same card without them (348.6 to 365.0 Hz, 76.5 c above the written note), and that alone takes the pitch measure outside its ruler (a gap of 93.4 Hz against 50.2). The render's peak, 20.49 Pa, is above the card's 16 Pa full scale, so 4090 positive peaks are clipped in that file. The passive chain of these rows puts the nose's first coupled peak at 374 Hz, 7 % above the note; that this peak pulled the fold up is an inference, not tested.

Viscothermal loss and a flanged-piston mouth load from the transfer-matrix duct; on the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes (not C3-a or F4-a) the head_load row adds the change of the head, with the torso under it below 10 kHz, to that load, and the mouth flow and the passive formants read the same load.

A measured yielding wall on the phrases and 10 of the 14 graded notes, including C4-u-rigid, whose name comes from an older comparison: per unit area 15.4 kg/m2, 3.79e5 Pa/m and 6.22e3 Pa s/m, from the wall inertance, tissue compliance and resistance Hanna, Smith and Wolfe (2016, Table III) measured in seven men through the lips with the glottis closed, in place of the Flanagan setting as given by Birkholz, Haesner and Kuerbis 2022 and its assumed stiffness. The wall alone took the notes 3.2 to 70.2 c off their pitch, so each of those cards' folds is retrimmed to the note for it by the card's own rule: fold stiffness only, pressure held, within 3 c of the written note, no recording. C3-a and F4-a, on the cards restored from 2026-11-05, and C4-a and F4-e, on their renders of 2026-11-08 before the wall (restored on 2026-11-10), carry the cited wall.

On the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes the tract holds alveolar air at 37 C, from the four partial pressures printed in OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 22.4, Table 22.3, with the argon inside the nitrogen as printed. Outside the lips, in the tracts of C3-a and F4-a (on the cards restored from 2026-11-05) and in the tracts of the older renders further down, the air is humid at body temperature. The medium is stationary and the lips' load stays the room's absolute impedance: the breath moved the tract's sound speed -1.19 %, and the passive first formants by -0.88 to -1.01 %, +0.18 to +0.31 % off that ratio; the wall and the losses don't scale with it either.
A 192 kHz fold clock on every page. The C3-a airway card was rendered at 240 kHz, the highest the flanged mouth load allows, but that render is not live since the restore of 2026-11-10.

Sound at the microphone, 0.30 m away at 45 degrees off axis: on the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes, the mouth is a cap of the opening's area on a rigid sphere of radius 8.7 cm for the head, over a rigid sphere of radius 16.9 cm for the torso, 5.3 cm between their surfaces (the KEMAR snowman of Algazi, Duda and Thompson 2002, in place of the 8.75 cm head alone of Brown and Duda 1998; the head's field from Morse and Ingard's cap-on-sphere series), blended back to the infinite baffle over 8-10 kHz; C3-a and F4-a (on the cards restored from 2026-11-05) and the older renders further down still radiate through a baffled circular opening. The torso is a mannequin's: torso change checked against an independent boundary-element solve at 250, 600, 1200 and 2400 Hz (within 1.68 %); above that it rests on the model's own convergence. The pressure inside the tract is never the output. On the same 12 notes and the phrases, each path from the mouth to the microphone also carries the absorption of the card's exterior air (the observer_law row): the oxygen and nitrogen vibrational relaxations of ISO 9613-1, with viscosity and heat conduction from the gas's own transport data; the head and torso still scatter without loss. Over 0.30 m it moves the served clips' 8 kHz third octave -0.015 to -0.010 dB re each clip's total, against -0.017 to -0.012 dB from ISO 9613-1 (13 pages; the grader started F4-o's cut 0.27 ms earlier, which moves its served clip more).

Slow pitch movement on the straight-tone notes and, under vibrato, on the phrases (Ternström and Friberg 1989 model; amplitude from choir singers told to sing straight), moving the fold stiffnesses (three on the two-mass cards, all four on the body-cover fold) and set for each two-mass card.

Fast pitch movement on the straight-tone notes, a second row in the same tension: the 18 to 33 Hz part of the movement Ternström and Friberg 1989 print for singers told to sing straight, 1.34 to 1.76 cents by vowel, read by eye from their Fig. 5, which is solid only to about 25 Hz and has no man at C4 or F4. It was sized once from each two-mass card's gain at 4 Hz and not iterated, so it reads 0.35 to 1.89 cents, the lowest on C4-u, and no recording enters. The recordings' fast movement looks like pitch at F4, but at C3 and C4 much of it doesn't, so part of what this row closes there may be noise in the recording.

Vibrato on the phrases only, with both pitch rows added under it on the same fold tension (adding them is a modelling choice; no print sets it): 5.9 Hz and +-69.5 cents, the means of 50 professional singers (Larrouy-Maestri, Magis and Morsomme 2014). The C4 phrase's tense /u/ swings +-260.9 cents on its render: the card's declared rescale doubles the depth at the halved tension-to-pitch gain, and near the tract's first resonance (264.4 Hz) the swing does not stay linear.

On the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes the glottal jet's noise comes from a measured duct-constriction law (the constriction_noise row: Oldham and Ukpoho 1990, K(St) measured on dampers and orifice plates, extrapolated to the glottis; no gain and no gate, its one number the radius of the first tract section), in place of the Verge 1995 flue-jet row. It is a substitution: both rows would count the jet twice. C3-a and F4-a, on the cards restored from 2026-11-05, carry the Verge row. The jet row's gate was a flow threshold: on the graded notes it sounded for part of each note at C4 and F4, only briefly at C3, and not at all on the C3 /i/ and /u/ pages, so there the law, which has no gate, adds the jet's noise; on the phrases it sounded for 0.7 to 11.2 % of each vowel at C3 and 19.5 to 28.0 % at C4. Part of the recordings' floor between the harmonics may be the room.

Pulse shimmer on the 14 graded notes and on the phrases: a per-cycle gain on the glottal pulse, sd 1.13 %, sized from the 1.28 % local shimmer Yoo et al. 2002 report for 65 classical singing students (abstract only; that figure's tracker floor wasn't taken out).
Breath pressure that rises over 150 ms, the centre of a speech range (Fant and Kruckenberg 2005), and is then held.

On C3-e and C4-o, a branched airway below the folds, the subglottal_airway row: Weibel's symmetric tree (1963) to 17 generations, with the dimensions Saab et al. print (2021, arXiv:2111.07627, Table 1, column B), from the trachea, 120 mm long and 18 mm across, to generation 17, 1.7 mm by 0.6 mm, each generation's 2^(n-1) tubes in parallel, with Bessel (Zwikker-Kosten) losses in the tract's gas and the card's breath pressure at the far end. It enters the glottis as a causal reflectance on its upstream side, and the fold forces take the pressure at its top. 17 is a convergence count, not a fit. The airway alone took the notes 0.8 to 314.4 c off their pitch; C4-a, C4-i, C4-o and F4-o were retrimmed to the note for it by the card's own rule (fold stiffness only, pressure held, within 3 c of the written note, no recording), and C3-e stayed within 3 c at the card's own stiffness. C4-a, C4-i and F4-o carried it from 2026-11-08 and play renders without it since 2026-11-10: C4-a's airway render (12 and 12, total distance 10.94) gave way on 2026-11-09 to the Tom tract and on 2026-11-10 to its render of 2026-11-08 before the wall and the airway (12 and 12, 10.85), and C4-i and F4-o went back to their wall renders by the owner's tie rule (C4-i 15 and 14, 9.49 against 9.69; F4-o 15 and 15, 5.84 against 6.37). The other nine pages were restored on 2026-11-10 to renders without the airway.

Folds retrimmed per card on the model alone: only the fold stiffnesses move (three on the two-mass cards, four on F4-a), no recording enters, and the tract's passive formants don't change. On C4-e the fold instead follows Ishizaka and Flanagan's printed tension law (1972, sec. 10.6): from their standard set, both masses and both thicknesses are divided by Q and the three springs multiplied by Q, with Q 1.6959 a setting chosen from the pitch of a first render and the breath pressure held. On that page the law leaves the glottal area's open and speed quotients where they were (open 0.764 against 0.769, speed 1.00 against 1.00, on a 4000 frame/s view of the fold trace), and its gain over the wall page is one measure, the spectral flux, inside its ruler by 2.1 %. Tried and not posted: on C3-a the law fell from 13 and 12 to 12 and 11 (the attack left its ruler), and on C4-i it tied 15 and 14 with the total distance growing (9.81 against 9.69, the airway page then live).

One listening page moves the tract within a note (the tract_move row): on C3 the subject's tense /a/ moves to the same subject's tense /i/ between 1.2 and 1.4 s, through 30 frozen shapes, each a log-area average of the two measured charts. It has no recording and no grade. Three limits: the glottal section is held constant, so the /i/ chart's first section takes the /a/ card's area; the mouth radius at the microphone stays the /a/ card's; and the shapes are frozen and crossfaded, coefficient interpolation between linear tracts, with no volume source from moving walls, which a real moving tract has.

One listening page says a word (the fricative_noise, tract_move and rest_gap rows), with Shadle's measured viscous term K3 at its /s/ constriction, less the Poiseuille resistance the tract line already carries (K3_eff): on C3 the subject's /a/ card says /sa/, with the same subject's measured /s/ as a keyframe, frication noise at its constriction, and the glottis opening and closing over time. It has no recording and no grade. Two stamped tests fail: with K3 the /s/ hold fell 0.58 dB where 3.1 dB was stamped (K3_eff then moves it 0.024 dB, as its own stamp said, with two of twelve bands outside their stamped steps), and the folds restart at a wider glottis than the human range. Three limits: the times are other speakers' and singers', the glottal gesture between its two measured instants is drawn linear, and the shapes are frozen and crossfaded.

One page renders the Dresden rig's printed model of subject 1's /s/ with no vocal folds, as the dataset measured it: the rig hole blown at the printed pressure, the printed trachea and bronchial horn below it, and supraglottal noise from Stevens' printed source at an obstacle (Acoustic Phonetics Fig. 2.33(a), on Shadle's 1985 data) placed at the incisors, measured on the same printed surface, and carried from Shadle's 2.54 cm tube into the tract's own section there by Shadle's eq. 3.3 area factor (+14.42 dB), both sudden expansions on one law (Ishizaka and Flanagan's eq. 6 at the hole, Borda-Carnot at the constriction), the constriction's measured viscous term K3 U in series with its kinetic drop (Shadle, RLE TR 506, eq. 2.2 and Table 2.2: 3.647 g/s-cm^4 at the tract's 0.134 cm^2, log-log between the printed circular plugs 1 cm long, less the tract line's own Poiseuille resistance over the sections the constriction spans, about 5.5 % of it), an unflanged thin-walled mouth and a free-field receiver at the rig microphone, at a 40 kHz clock.
physics_missing: The singer's own tract: on all 14 pages these are one man's spoken vowels, and larynx height, pharynx and lip shape differ in singing. The spectrum's tilt follows the subject's vowels, not the singers', and 1-2 kHz is further from the recordings than on the earlier cards on 11 of the 13 pages read before C4-a went back to this tract. A sung tract was tried on C4-a and is not live: a trained singer's sung /a/, Tom, Titze, Hoffman and Story (1999, NCVS Status and Progress Report 14:101-112), Table III, the C4 mp condition, 44 sections at the length Table IV measures for it, 17.29 cm; one 45-year-old man with Western classical training (12 years as a baritone, 6 as a countertenor), imaged by electron-beam CT, supine. The report's sung conditions are falsetto, while the card's fold is modal, and the report's piriform sinus wasn't on the card. Its passive formants sat 1.2 to 3.9 % above the authors' computed ones (Table VII). It posted on 2026-11-09 by the count rule, a tie at 12 of 15 (12 strict), with the measured wall and the branched airway; on 2026-11-10 the page went back by the owner's tie rule to its render of 2026-11-08 on the subject's tense /a/ (set voice/C4-a-foldshape), the same 12 and 12 with a smaller total distance, 10.85 against 12.67. The same singer's C4 ff tract scored 10 of 15 against 12 and wasn't posted, and on F4 the fold jumps over the note on both of the singer's tracts, so F4-a keeps its own.

The recordings' irregularity from one cycle to the next, a property of the recordings, not a row. On the grader 10 pages are cleaner than their recordings, by 0.98 dB (F4-e) to 12.82 dB (C4-e), and 4 are less clean, by 0.70 dB (F4-a) to 4.76 dB (C4-o); harmonics-to-noise is inside its loose ruler on all 14. Read on the served clips and the full recordings (2026-11-10): the recordings' floor before or after the note sits 37.4 to 59.6 dB under the note inside the grader's band, and taking it out moves a gap by at most 0.6 dB; shimmer moves the recordings' cycle-synchronous harmonics-to-noise by -0.54 to +1.08 dB; slow pitch movement moves the grader's harmonics-to-noise by at most 1.3 dB on the three pages tested (C4-e, C4-i, C3-a; read on the clips served before 2026-11-10 07:27Z), because the grader flattens the pitch before it reads. What stays is the recordings' period irregularity from one cycle to the next, local jitter 2 to 3 times the renders' on three of the cleanest notes (C3-u 0.41 against 0.15 %, C3-a 0.36 against 0.15 %, C4-e 0.20 against 0.07 %), and waveform change from one cycle to the next: with each cycle compared with its neighbours, a cycle-synchronous estimator rather than the grader's, the recordings stay 2.7 to 7.1 dB noisier than the renders on seven pages (C3-a 7.1, C4-e 6.8, C4-i 5.2, C3-e 4.4, C3-u 4.4, C4-a 4.1, C3-o 2.7 dB, read on the pages live at 07:23Z on 2026-11-10; C3-a, C4-a, C4-e and C4-i have since moved to other renders), and the four pages sung by singer m11 are among the five largest. Putting a recording's own period contour on the render lowers the render's harmonics-to-noise by 1.8 to 5.4 dB (C4-e, C4-i, C3-a), and taking it out of the recording raises the recording's by 1.0 to 6.7 dB (both read on the clips served before 2026-11-10 07:27Z); the two directions bound the share, they don't fix it. No noise row is added for the rest: the one measured noise of a glottis-shaped orifice found (Zhang, Mongeau, Frankel, Thomson and Park 2004, a static orifice in a duct) sits 24 to 29 dB under the card's constriction_noise row at 8 and 20 cm H2O, at 3.2 and 5.1 kHz. The printed aspiration level, tried on C3-o and C4-a, moved the floor by under .1 dB.

Words, consonants and moving tract shapes: fold settings are fixed within a render, each join between vowels in the phrases is a crossfade, and the one page that moves the tract within a note crossfades frozen shapes, each a log-area average of two measured charts. No articulatory model carries that move. Two linear models built on the subject's own MRI were tried between the tense /a/ and the tense /i/, and both missed their stamped predictions. Moved straight in its coefficients, a model of the midsagittal widths keeps both half-formed constrictions, with a single narrowing on 2 of 63 shapes; a model of the tongue contour does the same, on 5 of 63, with 4 shapes whose outline crosses itself. Both rest on 19 of the subject's 22 scans: the /e/, /o/ and "ich" scans could not be placed in a common frame. The width model's laws from midsagittal width to area miss the close vowels on their own: given the tense /u/'s measured widths, they put its second formant at 932 Hz, against 646 Hz from that scan's own cuts. The width model's halfway shape was rendered once on C3, held still, as a dose read: the largest second difference of its pressure at the microphone over 0.5-1.2 s is 1.930 times the /a/ card's, between the log-area halfway shape's 2.174 and the /i/ card's 1.256, and the 0.2 s windows of the two halfway shapes overlap (1.35-2.62 against the log-area shape's 1.63-2.44), so whether the depth of the half-formed constrictions causes the log-area halfway shape's excess over both ends is neither shown nor ruled out. A third model was read and not rendered: Story's (2005) two-mode vowel model, from another man's MRI. Under the paper's own Eq. 3, its printed Table IV coefficients close the tract at the lips on /i/ (0.031 cm2) and on /ʌ/ (0.010 cm2), with the /i/ shape's first two resonances near 100 and 620 Hz, although the same model reproduces the formant points of the paper's own Figs. 10 and 11. A 2009 erratum (J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 125, 1248) replaces Table IV's values; the replacement values have not been read.

No print sizes pitch movement under vibrato: the phrases carry the straight-tone sizes there. There are no register changes or formant-tuning gestures. Tested on cards that aren't posted: on the Tom 1999 F4 tract, with pressure held, the fold jumps over F4: from 330.90 Hz to 371.22 Hz as Q rises 0.516 % (mp), and from 326.81 to 367.00 Hz (ff); no Q holds the note. Observed: across the jump 2 f0 stays above the passive F1, 28.6 Hz above it on the mp low branch and 109.2 Hz on the high branch (F1 633.2 Hz), and 42.7 and 123.1 Hz on ff (F1 610.9 Hz).

The singers' tuning and pitch movement: the cards are trimmed to the written note, and on the grader the live pages sit -9.1 to +6.2 cents from equal temperament, while the recordings sit -48.3 to +10.0 cents from it. As read on 2026-11-09, before the restores, the period swing over the middle of a clip was 17.7 to 46.2 cents (5-95 %), against 11.5 to 100.6 cents in the recordings; it hasn't been read again on the restored pages.

A sung onset: the pressure rise is a speech value from one male speaker, and no adduction gesture is entered. The closest printed timings are spoken, not sung: for a modal /i/ by untrained speakers, 303 ms from the start of adduction to the final posture, held 106 ms before voicing (Shiba and Chhetri 2016), with no glottal widths printed. Attacks read 12.8 to 92.6 ms against 21.6 to 580.0 ms in the recordings.

Fold tissue: lumped cards, two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes and Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover on F4-a, not continuous layered tissue or a 3-D fold. The damping and collision values are printed typical values of one model each, not measurements of a voice, and one stiffness scale per card stands in for a fold-elongation law (on C4-e the scale follows Ishizaka and Flanagan's printed tension law, which moves masses, thicknesses and springs together; it is still one factor); the body-cover report moves pitch with Titze and Story's 2002 muscle rules, which aren't open. At its own rest area (5 mm²) the /sa/ card's fold starts on a slow pressure ramp at 169.6 Pa, under the spread of nine excised human larynges at vocal-process gaps of 0.5 to 1 mm (Mau et al. 2011; donors aged 62 to 92, gaps set by shims), and its onset rises linearly with the gap, as published two-mass models predict and the excised larynges do not. Its fold damping, read as in vacuo modal ratios (0.196 at 95 Hz, 0.218 at 150 Hz), is already at or above the in vivo human measurements (Kaneko et al. 1987, 0.12 at 100 Hz; Švec et al. 2000, 0.13 at 171 Hz), so a human damping value would lower the onset further, not close the gap. Setting those modes against the measured ones is a modelling step: the measurements are whole-fold modal ratios, and the card's are its in vacuo modes from per-mass damping, with no flow and linear springs, its first mode set against Kaneko's first eigenfrequency and its second against Švec's second mode.

Lungs and airway: the breath pressure is an authored player input on each card, not a measured one. Measured pressures were tried on three cards on 2026-11-10 and not posted: the median of Perrine and Scherer's three men at normal loudness (2023, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 154:1505, Tables III, V and VII; subglottal pressure read from the oral pressure during the /p/ occlusion), 7.76 cmH2O on C3-a (their normal pitch, the median man at 133 Hz) and 8.74 cmH2O on C4-e and C4-i (their higher pitch, the median man at 181 Hz, the nearest printed condition; no print found gives men at 261 Hz), in place of the authored 4.99, 18.73 and 20.35 cmH2O. Holmberg, Hillman and Perkell's 1988 values for 25 men were not found in an open copy. Each card was then retrimmed to its note by its own factor, a setting chosen from the pitch of a first render: C3-a's springs x 0.729, C4-e's Q 1.947, C4-i's springs x 1.611. Each count fell below the note's best: C3-a 11 and 10 against 14 and 14 (the card it was tried on, without the nasal rows, read 13 and 12), C4-e 9 and 9 against 10 and 10, C4-i 13 and 12 against 15 and 14. On a 4000 frame/s view of the fold trace, at C4 the open quotient came near that of the men Patel et al. (2026) filmed (0.86 on C4-e and 0.92 on C4-i, against 0.76 and 0.74 at the authored pressure) and the speed quotient moved further from theirs (0.90 and 0.83, against 1.00 and 1.00); the C3-a card's peak glottal flow was 915 cm3/s, 1.8 times the 507 ml/s of AC flow Perrine and Scherer measured in the man whose pressure it took. On two of the graded notes (C3-e and C4-o) it acts at the far end of a branched airway below the folds, with no lung tissue, chest wall or breathing movement behind it; the other twelve graded notes and the phrases keep the ideal port, the pressure straight under the glottis (C4-a, C4-i and F4-o carried the airway until 2026-11-10). The airway's walls are a stand-in, the card's vocal-tract wall (Hanna, Smith and Wolfe 2016): supraglottal, measured through the lips with the glottis closed, not subglottal. With that stand-in the computed airway load misses the measured one: the tree's input impedance peaks at 438, 1192 and 1899 Hz, at 22.99, 22.71 and 13.07 MPa s/m3, against 640, 1400 and 2100 Hz at 2.5 to 5 MPa s/m3 measured by Ishizaka, Matsudaira and Kaneko (1976), about 200 Hz low and 2.6 to 9.2 times too high. On the 14 graded notes, against byte-equal controls, the airway alone (before any retrim) took the loose count from 149 to 137 and the total distance from 165.52 to 180.53. A measured subglottal wall was tried on 2026-11-10, with no render, and is not carried: Habib et al.'s per-order wall thickness and cartilage fraction (1994, as reproduced in Aliboni's 2017 MSc thesis, Politecnico di Milano, Table 4), in vivo soft tissue (viscosity 102 Pa s, modulus 5.81e4 Pa; Aliboni et al. 2020, PLOS ONE, Table 2) and two nominal cartilage sets (Royston 2008; Aliboni et al. 2020). Each check was stated before it was computed, and neither passed. On Weibel's tree the first maximum came at 506 and 476 Hz, 21 and 26 % below 640 Hz, though the magnitudes, 3.55 to 5.88 MPa s/m3, came near the print. On a Horsfield tree from Habib's table below the MRI airway of Hanna et al. (2016), with the tissue terms Hanna et al. (2018) fitted to closed-glottis data, read at the lips against their subject 7's measured 210, 720 and 1100 Hz, the first three maxima came at 243 to 274, 587 to 724 and 1065 to 1302 Hz, and none of the four attachments and cartilage sets put all three within 10 %.

Tract acoustics beyond plane-wave sections: no cross-modes, and on every page but C3-a no nasal coupling or side branches; C3-a's nasal branch is plane-wave sections too. The sphenoidal and frontal sinuses are not carried. Printed sphenoidal ostia were found (Okumuş and Yurdabakan 2022, cone-beam CT of 240 scans: in men, mean horizontal diameters of 2.19 mm right and 2.29 mm left; Dang, Honda and Suzuki 1994, Sub.4: radii 0.098 and 0.130 cm, lengths 0.391 and 0.293 cm), but a check stated before it was computed failed. On the sphenoidal volumes of Sub.2, the subject whose passages and maxillary sinuses C3-a carries (12.1 and 5.2 cm3), the Helmholtz formula of Dang and Honda (1996, Eq. (6)) puts the two sinuses at 449 to 1049 Hz with either print (the cone-beam diameters taken with Sub.4's ostium lengths), 45 to 74 % below that subject's measured anti-resonances of 1750 and 1900 Hz, where 10 % was the pass. Applied to Sub.4's own ostia and volumes, the same formula falls 26 to 28 % short of the anti-resonances measured on the subject that matches Sub.4 by maxillary volume, and further off with that subject's sides swapped. A frontal ostium is printed for a population (Yang et al. 2004, CT of 80 patients: 7.3 by 8.5 mm) but not for these subjects (Dang, Honda and Suzuki could not measure it), and no printed length of the frontal drainage pathway was found, so the frontal sinus could not be checked.

The piriform fossae as side branches from the DVTD meshes were tested against the measured transfer functions on 8 tracts and failed the stamped gate (trough within 5 % on 0 of 8, band within 2 dB on 0 of 8). A full 3-D FE on the same meshes places the trough on 7 of 8 but stays 2-6 dB high on the 4-8 kHz band. DVTD subject 1's own FE problem, reproduced exactly on s1-02 and s1-17 (trough +0.00 %, bands +0.00 dB), keeps its 4.10 and 4.19 kHz troughs with the whole piriform region cut out: moved 0.00 % and +0.23 %, 9.2 and 12.9 dB shallower. The fossae deepen those troughs but do not set their frequencies, so no side-branch row places them and none is added. The measured and FE troughs were read before this test's rules were written.

The tract above 4 kHz on rounded vowels: on the subject's /o/ and /u/ tracts the cards' one-dimensional chain carries 5.7 to 9.9 dB more at 4-8 kHz than the measured transfer of the same 3-D print, against -0.6 to +3.3 dB on the subject's five unrounded vowels. Under the FE's own laws the same chain sits 1.2 to 7.2 dB over the 3-D FE of the same mesh on the rounded tracts, most of it at 4-5 kHz, and 0.4 to 5.3 dB under it on the unrounded ones, so on three of the four much of the excess is the plane-wave model itself, not the cut. None of the cuts tried (levels of a potential, centreline planes, geodesic shells), and not the paper's lip load, brings any rounded tract within 2 dB at 4-8 kHz.

The wall's detail: it's uniform along the tract, not a measured distribution, and its values are the mean of seven men measured through the lips, not this singer's or the subject's, uncertain by about 35 % on the mass and 50 % on the stiffness; one man's cheek and neck, measured with a shaker on the skin (Ishizaka, French and Flanagan 1975), span 15 to 24 kg/m2 and 8.0e3 to 2.32e4 Pa s/m. The subject's first formants on these cards sit 46 to 72 Hz above the print's measured ones. That gap is the wall, 37 C air (alveolar on 12 of the 14 cards, humid on C3-a and F4-a) and, by .2 to 1.5 Hz on the renders before the breath, the load of the head and torso at the lips, against a rigid model at room temperature, and the wall hasn't been split from the air.

A singer's torso, the neck, the outer nose and the lips' shape: the phrases and 12 of the 14 graded notes have a rigid spherical head over a rigid spherical torso, the KEMAR snowman of Algazi, Duda and Thompson 2002, and nothing else; C3-a and F4-a have neither and radiate from an infinite baffle. KEMAR is a mannequin; the print says a sphere is not a good approximation of the human torso, particularly at low elevations, and it computed the snowman from 0 to 5 kHz. The mouth on the head's horizontal equator facing front, with the microphone at mouth height, is a choice no print makes. On those 12 notes and the phrases the lips see the head's own radiation load: the head_load row (the cap on the same sphere, Morse and Ingard 1968 sec. 7.2) on top of the flanged pipe's, which lowered the grade by one row in 135; the torso's change to that load and to the microphone's pressure, below 10 kHz, moved the grade from 134 to 136 rows in 204. Above 10 kHz the pressure is the baffle's. The receiver's resolved band is 8 kHz, so energy above that isn't a prediction. On F4-a the head, the torso and the head_load row were tried alone on 2026-11-10 and not posted: added to its live body-cover card with no other row moved and no retrim, on a binary that renders the card without them byte for byte as the page's raw render, they read 8 and 8 against the note's best of 9 and 9 (total distance 13.6821 against 10.6039). Against the same card without them, the partials below 800 Hz fell 4.1 dB and those at 2 to 3.5 kHz 0.9 dB, the spectral centroid moved from 1080 to 1321 Hz against the recording's 897, and the spectral distance left its ruler; the pitch moved -4.0 c.

The breath's onset: a held vowel's first breath is dead-space air, mixed toward room air, before the expired air is alveolar, and the twelve cards with alveolar air hold it from the first sample. The breath doesn't mix with the room at the lips, and the room itself is a declared state, humid air at 37 C, not a measured one.

Convergence of the fold clock, run on the C3-a card as it stood before the branched airway (card d306b358; 2026-11-10, music_render 2733eb8c5db0, only the audio row's fold ratio changed): rungs N = 2, 3, 4, 5 (96 to 240 kHz) give mean f0 130.78454, 130.84821, 130.87932 and 130.89642 Hz over 1.0 to 2.8 s, steps of +0.84, +0.41 and +0.23 cents, and level steps under 0.006 dB. A fit f0(N) = f_inf + C N^-p over the four rungs gives order p 1.133 (1.053 to 1.215) and f_inf 130.958 Hz, so N=4 (192 kHz, the clock of the other voice pages) sits 1.04 cents below that limit and N=5 0.82 cents below; both figures are extrapolations from rungs at or below 240 kHz. Not converged in the third octaves 3.2 to 5 kHz: from N=4 to N=5 they still move 0.25 to 0.60 dB, over the 0.12 dB stamped before the rungs ran, while bands up to 2.5 kHz move at most 0.09 dB. N=5 is the top rung on this card: the flanged mouth load refuses above ka 28.0, and this 12.95 mm mouth reaches ka 27.39 at N=5. The C3-a airway card was rendered at N=5: from N=4 its pitch moves +0.28 cents and its 3.2 kHz third octave 0.51 dB, and the grader's count stays 10 of 15; that render is not live, since C3-a was restored on 2026-11-10 to its 192 kHz card of 2026-11-05, whose nasal render is also at 192 kHz. The other tract cards have no ladder of their own.

A noise source, a constriction flow law and a radiation measured in a fricative's own range: the /s/ page applies Stevens' U^3 rule as printed, although the figure's own two curves imply U^1.89 to U^2.78, at flows of 506 to 902 cm^3/s against the figure's 160 and 420, with its obstacle 12.1 mm from the constriction against the figure's 3 cm, and renders 11.6 dB under the rig's recording at 0.5 W (11.7 dB under with the whole K3, 9.0 dB under before the K3 term). In Shadle's own rig, rendered before the K3 term with the obstacle case at lf 3.2 and 12 cm at Table 4.1's four flows, the same source renders louder than Table 4.1 by +3.1 to +7.4 dB, so the gap is not one scale factor; those cards differ from Shadle's rig in three declared ways: the tapered inlet is not modelled, the obstacle is a half-area plane section, and the glottal end is an orifice off a held pressure where the rig's was reflectionless. The constriction's K3 is read off Table 2.2's circular plugs 1 cm long, 3.647 g/s-cm^4; the same table read other ways gives 6.986 (the rectangular plugs) and 2.394 (Shadle's stated K3 proportional to lc / Ac^2, over the tract's sections narrower than 0.318 cm^2). The measured K3 includes the Poiseuille flow inside the plug, and the tract line already carries the Poiseuille resistance of its own sections, so the constriction takes K3 less that resistance over the sections it spans, the run through the constriction narrower than 0.318 cm^2: sections 81 to 86, about 5.5 % of K3 (8.4 % of the printed 8.7 g/s-cm^4 on Shadle's 0.079 cm^2 plug), computed from the card's sections and the tract gas's own viscosity; the subtraction raised the level 0.1 dB at every power. Outside the printed 0.020 to 0.318 cm^2 the rule continues by Shadle's stated 1 / Ac^2, an extrapolation Shadle warns of (p. 39: "Recognize that extrapolation to other constrictions or ranges of U may be inaccurate."); this page's 0.134 cm^2 lies inside. The plane-wave model has no obstacle beyond its area change and no directivity (a bound of about 3 dB at the rig microphone's 45 deg), so where the gap comes from is not located. The duct-area factor scales the noise source alone. On the render before the K3 term, at 0.5 W the render departs from the render without the factor, multiplied by the factor, in two places, where the content is not the source's: in the onset (the departure lies 10.0 dB under the render over the first 0.1 s) and below 63 Hz (3.2 to 5.9 dB under in each third octave). The grade's scalogram difference was predicted to stay at 17.41 dB; it read 17.55 dB on that render.

Fricative tracts from Story (2005), tried and not rendered. Story's printed fit (Table I's values on Table III's modes, the constriction of Eqs. 3, 5, 6 and 9, with Eqs. 7 and 8 read from Fig. 4 and the text, which they disagree with as printed), rebuilt, sits as close to Story's Table V area functions of /f/, /θ/, /s/ and /ʃ/ as Story's Fig. 8 prints: R 0.79 to 0.94 and rms 0.43 to 0.93 cm2, each within 0.036 in R and 0.041 cm2 in rms of Fig. 8's values. The shapes are fitted values, fitted to another man's MRI, not measured on the subject, and Story writes that these images "are not adequate to provide information for aerodynamic modeling of turbulence generation". Table V as printed is refused by the fricative route: /θ/ and /ʃ/ have a closed section, and /f/ and /s/ are narrowest at the lips. The fitted /θ/, /s/ and /ʃ/ were refused at the glottis: their first sections, 0.21 to 0.31 cm2, are narrower than the rig's 0.78 cm2 hole, and Stevens' estimate of a fricative's glottal opening under the intraoral pressure, about 0.30 cm2 (Acoustic Phonetics, Fig. 8.2: an estimate, not a measurement), still refuses /s/ and /ʃ/. The fitted /s/ also narrows to 0.058 cm2 at its fifth section, from Story's neutral tract, where Table V's MRI has 0.94 cm2.

A tense /u/ on C4: the subject's tense /u/ tract was tried on C4-u and C4-u-rigid and took each page from 14 to 8 inside the loose rulers, its 1 to 4 kHz bands about 20 dB under the lax page's. The lax tract stays.

The measured wall's effect on F4-a: tried with its pitch retrim, the F4-a render fell from 7 to 4 inside the loose rulers against the render just before it, both graded on 2026-11-10. The cause is not separated: the control meant to put the pitch back missed it by 10 cents. Neither render is live; F4-a plays its restored render of 2026-11-05.

No row for cycle-to-cycle period jitter: the two prints found for trained singers (Baker et al. 2023, RAP 0.129 %, pooled sexes; Rasch 1983, two singers, 13 to 37 c for a baritone) disagree by 5 to 8 times.
